description: FAYNOVA is a passionate and ambitious team driven by curiosity and a shared love for science, space, and technology. Our team consists of two members, Avina Tabarestani and Aynour Eghtedayi, who combine their ideas, skills, and determination to explore innovative solutions to real-world challenges. Through NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to turn our curiosity into meaningful discoveries and push the boundaries of what we can achieve. We believe every great discovery begins with an idea!
summary: What happens to fire when gravity becomes very small? We made Flame Guard to explore this question and share what we learned. Our browser project combines an interactive flame lab, a collection of combustion experiment records, charts, NASA images, and a science guide. Visitors can choose experiment presets, filter records, compare available measurements, and save selected results. A built-in assistant answers basic questions about the project and its data. The flame animations help explain ideas, while the records offer a separate way to explore experiments. We want to make NASA microgravity combustion research easier to understand and encourage curiosity about fire safety in space.
details:
We started with a question: why can fire look so different in space? Understanding these differences is part of learning how to keep future space missions safer. Flame Guard connects this question to NASA combustion research through activities that visitors can explore for themselves.

Our current project includes seven flame presets inspired by experiments such as FLEX, BASS, SoFIE, Saffire, and ACME. Visitors can rotate the flame view, explore 1,284 records across seven dataset groups, search and filter the tables, and compare available oxygen, pressure, and burn-duration measurements. Charts, Excel exports, and printable tables help visitors keep exploring. NASA images, a science guide, and a built-in question-and-answer assistant add context.

We used HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Canvas to bring these activities together in one file. Our creative idea is to connect seeing a flame, asking a question, and exploring experiment records in the same place. The animated flames are educational illustrations; the charts describe the included records. The project is a learning tool rather than a fire-safety prediction system.
